```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 120, out.width = "100%", raster3d = 3e4, dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg",
  dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
PAL <- c(blue = "#2E6F9E", red = "#B5342B", green = "#3F7A3D",
         orange = "#9E5E0F", purple = "#7A4F9E", teal = "#2A7A7A",
         grey = "#5C6166")
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 17) + theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.key = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.box.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.position = "none"))
```

A geom draws a shape from mapped data. A stat computes new values or geometry before drawing. This article gives small examples of the geoms and stats that draw data rows: points, paths, gridded surfaces, columns, distributions, intervals and reference geometry. Installation is covered in [Get started](ggplot3d.html). [Surfaces, solids and fields](surfaces-solids.html) covers meshes, function and fitted surfaces, level surfaces, hulls, solid glyphs and sweeps. [Vector fields](vector-fields.html) covers arrows and streamlines, and [Implicit surfaces](implicit-surfaces.html) covers reconstruction from point clouds.

## Points, paths, segments and text

Each row below contains a position and a label. Points draw one mark per row. Paths connect rows in their input order within each group.

```{r points, fig.alt="Three blue points in three dimensions."}
d <- data.frame(x = c(0, 1, 2), y = c(0, 2, 1), z = c(1, 3, 2),
                label = c("a", "b", "c"))
p <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y, z = z))
p + geom_point_3d(size = 3, colour = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d()
```

```{r paths, fig.alt="A blue path connecting the same three positions in input order."}
p + geom_path_3d(linewidth = 0.8, colour = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d()
```

Segments use a start and an endpoint from each row. Text places labels at the mapped positions. A dropline joins each position to the selected face of the data box.

```{r segments, fig.alt="Three blue segments dropping to z equal to zero."}
p + geom_segment_3d(aes(xend = x, yend = y, zend = 0),
                     linewidth = 0.8, colour = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d()
```

```{r text, fig.alt="The labels a, b and c at three positions."}
p + geom_text_3d(aes(label = label), size = 5) + coord_3d()
```

Text outlines can lie in a plane through each anchor. `normal` gives its
direction in normalized panel coordinates; `up` gives the reading-up hint.
The frame and aspect scaling transform those directions into the displayed
model. `angle` rotates within the plane.

```{r tilted-text, fig.alt="Font outlines lying on tilted planes through three anchors."}
p + geom_text_3d(aes(label = label), orientation = "plane",
  normal = c(1, 1, 1), up = c(0, 0, 1), size = 8) + coord_3d()
```

`facing = "camera_plane"` gives the outlines a shared view-facing direction.
`facing = "camera_point"` turns each label toward the perspective eye from
its own anchor. Each panel resolves its orientation using its drawing camera;
the HTML viewer updates it during orbit and playback. The outlines participate
in the scene's depth testing and picking.

```{r camera-text, fig.alt="Font outlines facing the perspective camera at three anchors."}
p + geom_text_3d(aes(label = label), orientation = "plane",
  facing = "camera_point", size = 8) + coord_3d(projection = "perspective")
```

```{r droplines, fig.alt="Three points with lines connecting them to the floor of the box."}
p + geom_dropline_3d(face = "zmin", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 3) + coord_3d()
```

## Polygons and bands

A polygon is an ordered ring of vertices in a plane after position transformations; the triangle below lies on a sloping plane. Use a group for each feature and a subgroup for each ring when a feature has holes.

```{r polygon, fig.alt="A blue triangular polygon in a sloping plane."}
triangle <- data.frame(x = c(0, 1, 0), y = c(0, 0, 1), z = c(0, 1, 1))
ggplot(triangle, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_polygon_3d(fill = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d()
```

A band joins two boundaries. Mapping zmin and zmax produces a vertical wall along the x/y path. Six endpoint aesthetics can describe a band with boundaries that also differ in x and y.

```{r band, fig.alt="A blue vertical band following a sine curve."}
band <- data.frame(x = seq(0, 4, length.out = 16), y = 0)
band$low <- sin(band$x)
band$high <- band$low + 0.5
ggplot(band, aes(x, y, zmin = low, zmax = high)) +
  geom_band_3d(fill = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d()
```

## Surfaces and contours

A gridded surface connects adjacent pairs of x/y coordinates with triangles. Scattered points can use Delaunay triangulation, which connects nearby points in the transformed x/y plane, with `method = "delaunay"`. Within each group, each x/y pair must be unique.

```{r surface, fig.alt="A curved blue surface sampled on a regular grid."}
surface <- expand.grid(x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 10),
                       y = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 10))
surface$z <- with(surface, exp(-(x^2 + y^2) / 2))
s <- ggplot(surface, aes(x, y, z = z))
s + geom_surface_3d(fill = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d()
```

The surface stat exposes the triangulation step. The computed height `z_mean` is the mean height of each triangle and can be mapped to fill after the stat has run.

```{r stat-surface, fig.alt="A curved surface coloured by each triangle's mean height."}
s + stat_surface_3d(aes(fill = after_stat(z_mean))) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#DCEAF3", high = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d()
```

Contours trace equal heights. Filled contours draw bands between height thresholds. The plane argument chooses the surface, the floor, or a fixed height in original units.

```{r contours, fig.alt="Height contours on a curved surface."}
s + geom_contour_3d(bins = 4, linewidth = 0.8) + coord_3d()
```

```{r filled-contours, fig.alt="Filled height bands projected onto the floor of the data box."}
s + geom_contour_filled_3d(bins = 4, plane = "floor") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = unname(PAL[c("blue", "teal", "green", "orange", "purple")])) +
  coord_3d()
```

## Images and textures

An image draped over a surface carries detail that would otherwise need a mesh as fine as the image. `texture` takes a `texture_3d()` image, or anything it reads (a colour matrix, a numeric array from `png::readPNG()`, a PNG file). Each face shows the image at its texture coordinates, which default to the x and y positions spread over the image; `extent` places the image in data units instead, and faces outside it keep their fill.

```{r drape, raster3d = TRUE, fig.alt="The volcano height map draped with a checkerboard image whose squares bend over the slopes."}
volcano_grid <- expand.grid(x = seq_len(nrow(volcano)), y = seq_len(ncol(volcano)))
volcano_grid$z <- as.vector(volcano)
coarse <- volcano_grid[volcano_grid$x %% 3 == 1 & volcano_grid$y %% 3 == 1, ]
checker <- matrix("#F2EFE6", 8, 8)
checker[(row(checker) + col(checker)) %% 2 == 1] <- "#2B5F75"
ggplot(coarse, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(texture = texture_3d(checker, interpolate = FALSE)) + coord_3d()
```

An image can also lie on a plane of the panel box. `geom_raster_3d()` turns values on a regular grid into one image, one per level of the remaining axis, and `annotation_raster_3d()` lays a given image on a plane. Both are single faces of the scene, so they are foreshortened and hidden like any other face; here the full-resolution height map lies on the floor under the coarse surface.

```{r raster-planes, raster3d = TRUE, fig.alt="The coarse volcano surface above a full-resolution coloured height map on the floor of the box and a colour ramp image on its back wall."}
ggplot(coarse, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_raster_3d(aes(fill = z), data = volcano_grid, at = -Inf) +
  annotation_raster_3d(matrix(grDevices::hcl.colors(8, "Zissou 1"), 1), plane = "xz", at = Inf) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey85", colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  coord_3d()
```

## Columns, counts and extrusions

Columns occupy cells on an x/y lattice and extend from a baseline to z. A bar layer counts observations at each x/y combination. The count stat gives direct access to that calculation.

```{r columns, fig.alt="Nine blue columns with heights from one to nine."}
columns <- expand.grid(x = 1:3, y = 1:3)
columns$z <- seq_len(nrow(columns))
ggplot(columns, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_col_3d(fill = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d()
```

```{r bars, fig.alt="Columns showing counts of cars by cylinder and gear categories."}
counts <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(factor(cyl), factor(gear)))
counts + geom_bar_3d(fill = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d()
```

```{r stat-count, fig.alt="The count stat drawing counts of cars by cylinder and gear categories."}
counts + stat_count_3d(fill = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d()
```

Two continuous variables are binned first. `geom_histogram_3d()` counts observations in rectangles and `geom_hex_3d()` in hexagons, drawn as hexagonal prisms. `stat_summary_2d_3d()` and `stat_summary_hex_3d()` bin the same way and set each height to a summary of z, the mean by default.

```{r hex, fig.alt="Hexagonal prisms counting Old Faithful eruptions by duration and waiting time, coloured by count."}
ggplot(faithful, aes(eruptions, waiting)) +
  geom_hex_3d(aes(fill = after_stat(count)), bins = 12) + coord_3d()
```

Extrusion extends an ordered x/y polygon between two heights. The z value gives its endpoint. The `base` argument supplies the starting height; a mapped zmin overrides it. Caps close the top and bottom.

```{r extrusion, fig.alt="A blue rectangular polygon extruded to a height of two."}
ring <- data.frame(x = c(0, 2, 2, 0), y = c(0, 0, 1, 1), z = 2)
ggplot(ring, aes(x, y, z = z)) + geom_extrude_3d(fill = PAL["blue"]) +
  coord_3d()
```

Stacking accumulates column heights separately above and below zero. It requires a linear continuous z scale and a shared zero baseline. Nudging shifts positions in transformed units.

```{r positions, fig.alt="Two coloured column sections stacked at a single x/y position."}
stack <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 1, z = c(2, 3), part = c("a", "b"))
ggplot(stack, aes(x, y, z = z, fill = part)) +
  geom_col_3d(position = position_stack_3d()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange")])) + coord_3d()
```

## Distributions at x/y positions

The iris data record flower measurements in centimetres for three species. Place each species at one x position and use petal length as the distribution along z. A boxplot draws a prism between the quartiles, a median face, whiskers and individual outliers.

```{r boxplots, fig.alt="Three box prisms summarising petal length for the iris species, with whiskers and outlier points."}
flowers <- ggplot(iris, aes(Species, y = 0, z = Petal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1), breaks = NULL, name = NULL)
flowers + geom_boxplot_3d(width = 0.6, depth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange", "teal")])) +
  coord_3d()
```

A violin shows the estimated density along z. The default wall mirrors that density along x; a revolved violin surrounds the vertical axis. Use discrete positions, or an explicit group for each numeric x/y cell.

```{r violin-wall, fig.alt="Three flat violin walls showing the petal-length distributions of the iris species."}
flowers + geom_violin_3d(shape = "wall", n = 32) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange", "teal")])) +
  coord_3d()
```

```{r violin-solid, fig.alt="The same three petal-length densities drawn as solid violins around their vertical axes."}
flowers + geom_violin_3d(shape = "revolve", n = 32, sides = 12) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange", "teal")])) +
  coord_3d()
```

## Waterfalls and stacked areas

A waterfall draws each group as a curtain from a baseline to its heights, ordered by x. Take three cross-sections of the built-in volcano elevation matrix. Each section occupies its own y position, with elevations measured in metres.

```{r waterfall, fig.alt="Three filled elevation profiles from the volcano matrix, separated along y and rising from a 90 metre baseline."}
profiles <- expand.grid(x = seq(1, nrow(volcano), by = 4), y = c(15, 30, 45))
profiles$z <- volcano[cbind(profiles$x, profiles$y)]
ggplot(profiles, aes(x, y, z = z, group = y, fill = factor(y))) +
  geom_waterfall_3d(base = 90) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange", "teal")])) +
  coord_3d()
```

An area wall stacks groups that share an x lattice and a y position. The built-in US personal expenditure table records spending in billions of dollars. Place its five spending categories on one wall, with year along x and expenditure along z. Positive and negative values stack separately from zero.

```{r stacked-area, fig.alt="Five spending categories stacked in a single wall over the five years of the US personal expenditure table."}
spending <- as.data.frame(as.table(USPersonalExpenditure))
names(spending) <- c("category", "year", "expenditure")
spending$year <- as.numeric(as.character(spending$year))
ggplot(spending, aes(year, y = 0, z = expenditure,
                     group = category, fill = category)) +
  geom_area_3d() + scale_fill_manual(values = unname(PAL[1:5]),
    labels = c("Food & tobacco", "Household", "Medical", "Personal care", "Education")) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 3)) +
  coord_3d() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The default area position is [position_stack_3d()](../reference/position_stack_3d.html). Choose [position_fill_3d()](../reference/position_stack_3d.html) to show proportions at each x position. Wall stacking requires a linear continuous z scale and a common zero baseline.

## Intervals and summaries

An interval layer accepts lower and upper bounds on any combination of x, y and z. Summarise iris petal length at each species position with a mean and an interval extending one standard error on either side.

```{r summary-intervals, fig.alt="Mean petal length with one-standard-error point ranges for each iris species."}
ggplot(iris, aes(Species, y = 0, z = Petal.Length)) +
  stat_summary_3d(fun.data = mean_se, colour = PAL["blue"], linewidth = 0.8) +
  coord_3d()
```

Summary tables containing cells with a single observation can currently fail
with `numbers of columns of arguments do not match`. For those tables,
compute the summaries first and pass their bounds to an interval layer.

For supplied intervals, map both bounds of each axis. Here a small table gives three measured positions with stated x, y and z uncertainties. Cross-shaped caps extend along both perpendicular axes, so the endpoints remain visible as the camera turns.

```{r errorbars, fig.alt="Three measured positions with capped uncertainty intervals along all three axes."}
measurements <- data.frame(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(2, 1, 3), z = c(3, 4, 2))
intervals <- ggplot(measurements, aes(x, y, z = z,
  xmin = x - 0.2, xmax = x + 0.2, ymin = y - 0.3, ymax = y + 0.3,
  zmin = z - 0.5, zmax = z + 0.5))
intervals + geom_errorbar_3d(width = 0.12, cap.plane = "cross",
                            linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 2.5, colour = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d()
```

[geom_linerange_3d()](../reference/geom_errorbar_3d.html) draws the interval segments, and [geom_pointrange_3d()](../reference/geom_errorbar_3d.html) adds their centres. A crossbar draws a box and marks the centre with a line. Restrict this example to z bounds to see that box clearly.

```{r crossbars, fig.alt="Three crossbar boxes spanning the supplied z intervals, with a line at each centre."}
ggplot(measurements, aes(x, y, z = z, zmin = z - 0.5, zmax = z + 0.5)) +
  geom_crossbar_3d(width = 0.25, cap.plane = "cross", fill = PAL["blue"]) +
  coord_3d()
```

A stem connects each position to a fixed value on one axis. Here each car's fuel consumption is connected to zero. Change the base or map an endpoint to give individual stems different starting values.

```{r stems, fig.alt="Fuel consumption for the cars as vertical stems from zero, with a point at each observed value."}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, hp, z = mpg)) +
  geom_stem_3d(base = 0, colour = PAL["blue"], linewidth = 0.7) + coord_3d()
```

## Reference lines and dimensions

Fix two intercepts to draw a reference line along the remaining axis. For an arbitrary line, supply a point and direction in transformed scale units; the line is cut to the box.

```{r reference-lines, fig.alt="Three points with a vertical reference line and an oblique diagonal through the box."}
p + geom_point_3d(size = 3) +
  geom_refline_3d(xintercept = 1, yintercept = 1, colour = PAL["red"]) +
  geom_abline_3d(point = c(0, 0, 1), direction = c(1, 1, 1),
                 colour = PAL["blue"], linetype = 2) +
  annotate_3d("text", x = 1, y = 1, z = 3, label = "reference", size = 5) +
  coord_3d()
```

Fixed segments can be added with [annotate_3d()](../reference/annotate_3d.html). Supply all three coordinates at each end. This arrow joins the first and last positions in the point table.

```{r annotation-segment, fig.alt="Three points with a blue arrow joining the first position at zero, zero, one to the last at two, one, two."}
p + geom_point_3d(size = 3) +
  annotate_3d("segment", x = 0, y = 0, z = 1,
    xend = 2, yend = 1, zend = 2, colour = PAL["blue"], linewidth = 0.8,
    arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(3, "mm"))) + coord_3d()
```

Annotate a fixed span with `annotate_3d("bracket", ...)`. The two endpoints use data coordinates; the offset uses fractions of the box dimensions. These examples label a supplied distance, with extension lines and arrowheads on the dimension version. Use [geom_bracket_3d()](../reference/geom_bracket_3d.html) to map spans from a data table.

```{r bracket, fig.alt="Two points connected by a bracket labelled span."}
span <- ggplot(data.frame(x = c(0, 2), y = 0, z = 1), aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 3)
span + annotate_3d("bracket", x = 0, y = 0, z = 1, xend = 2, yend = 0, zend = 1,
  label = "span", size = 5, offset = c(0, 0, 0.12)) +
  coord_3d(clip_data = FALSE)
```

```{r dimension, fig.alt="Two points with a dimension line and extension lines labelled 2 m."}
span + annotate_3d("bracket", x = 0, y = 0, z = 1, xend = 2, yend = 0, zend = 1,
  type = "dimension", label = "2 m", size = 5,
  offset = c(0, -0.12, 0)) + coord_3d(clip_data = FALSE)
```

## Reference and clipping planes

A reference plane marks a threshold through the box. An oblique plane takes a normal vector and a point on the plane; for the plane z = a + b x + c y, use the normal (-b, -c, 1) and point (0, 0, a).

```{r reference-plane, fig.alt="The curved surface intersected by a translucent horizontal plane at height one half."}
s + geom_surface_3d(fill = PAL["blue"]) +
  geom_plane_3d(zintercept = 0.5, fill = PAL["orange"], alpha = 0.4) + coord_3d()
```

A clipping plane keeps the half-space its normal points into. Close a cut solid by enabling its cap. Here the normal points towards positive y, leaving the part of a sphere at y greater than or equal to zero.

```{r clipping-plane, fig.alt="A sphere cut in half at y equal to zero, with a flat cap closing the cut."}
ggplot(data.frame(x = 0, y = 0, z = 0), aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_sphere_3d(radius = 1, detail = 2, fill = PAL["teal"]) +
  coord_3d(aspect = "data", clip_planes = list(
    clip_plane_3d(normal = c(0, 1, 0), point = c(y = 0), cap = TRUE)))
```

The coordinate's clipping planes apply to every layer. A layer's own plane list replaces that list; an empty list keeps the layer whole. Open surfaces receive caps only where the cut forms a closed outline. See [clip_plane_3d()](../reference/clip_plane_3d.html) for the plane conventions.

## Adapting a layer

The layer adapter equips a registered ggplot2 geom with three-dimensional scene emission. Extension authors register an emitter to describe how another geom produces geometry. The registration help page describes the callback arguments.

```{r adapter, fig.alt="Three points drawn by an adapted ggplot2 point layer."}
p + layer_3d(geom_point(size = 3)) + coord_3d()
```
